questions.question: Let $D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ and let $f\colon D\to\mathbb{R}$ be a function. Which subset of $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ is the epigraph $\operatorname{Epi}(f)$?
options: $\{(\boldsymbol{x},y)\in\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}\colon \boldsymbol{x}\in D,\ y\leq f(\boldsymbol{x})\}$
$\{(\boldsymbol{x},y)\in\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}\colon \boldsymbol{x}\in D,\ y\geq f(\boldsymbol{x})\}$
$\{(\boldsymbol{x},y)\in\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}\colon \boldsymbol{x}\in D,\ y=f(\boldsymbol{x})\}$
$\{(\boldsymbol{x},y)\in\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}\colon \boldsymbol{x}\in D,\ y>f(\boldsymbol{x})\}$

questions.question: Let $D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be a convex set and $f\colon D\to\mathbb{R}$. Which statement correctly links the function $f$ with the set $\operatorname{Epi}(f)$?
options: $f$ is concave if and only if $\operatorname{Epi}(f)$ is a convex set.
If $f$ is convex then $\operatorname{Epi}(f)$ is convex, but not conversely.
$f$ is convex if and only if $\operatorname{Epi}(f)$ is a convex set.
$f$ is convex if and only if $\operatorname{Epi}(f)$ is a closed set.

questions.question: Let $D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be nonempty and let $f,g\colon D\to\mathbb{R}$ satisfy $f(\boldsymbol{x})<g(\boldsymbol{x})$ for every $\boldsymbol{x}\in D$. Which set is the difference $\operatorname{Epi}(f)\setminus\operatorname{Epi}(g)$?
options: $\{(\boldsymbol{x},y)\colon \boldsymbol{x}\in D,\ f(\boldsymbol{x})\leq y<g(\boldsymbol{x})\}$
$\{(\boldsymbol{x},y)\colon \boldsymbol{x}\in D,\ f(\boldsymbol{x})\leq y\leq g(\boldsymbol{x})\}$
$\{(\boldsymbol{x},y)\colon \boldsymbol{x}\in D,\ y\geq g(\boldsymbol{x})\}$
$\{(\boldsymbol{x},y)\colon \boldsymbol{x}\in D,\ g(\boldsymbol{x})\leq y<f(\boldsymbol{x})\}$

questions.question: Let $f\colon\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ be convex, so that $\operatorname{Epi}(f)$ is a convex set. Which statement about the graph $\{(x,f(x))\colon x\in\mathbb{R}\}$ of $f$ is correct?
options: It is convex, because it is a subset of the convex set $\operatorname{Epi}(f)$.
It is convex, because it collects the lowest point of each vertical slice of $\operatorname{Epi}(f)$.
It is never convex, because the graph of a convex function always curves upwards.
It need not be convex: it is only the lower boundary of the convex set $\operatorname{Epi}(f)$.

questions.question: Let $D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be convex, $f\colon D\to\mathbb{R}$, $\boldsymbol{x}_1\neq\boldsymbol{x}_2$ in $D$ and $0<\lambda<1$. In general, the point $\lambda(\boldsymbol{x}_1,f(\boldsymbol{x}_1))+(1-\lambda)(\boldsymbol{x}_2,f(\boldsymbol{x}_2))$ lies in $\operatorname{Epi}(f)$ exactly when which inequality holds?
options: $f(\lambda\boldsymbol{x}_1+(1-\lambda)\boldsymbol{x}_2)\geq\lambda f(\boldsymbol{x}_1)+(1-\lambda)f(\boldsymbol{x}_2)$
$f(\lambda\boldsymbol{x}_1+(1-\lambda)\boldsymbol{x}_2)\leq\max\{f(\boldsymbol{x}_1),f(\boldsymbol{x}_2)\}$
$f(\lambda\boldsymbol{x}_1+(1-\lambda)\boldsymbol{x}_2)\leq\lambda f(\boldsymbol{x}_1)+(1-\lambda)f(\boldsymbol{x}_2)$
$f(\lambda\boldsymbol{x}_1+(1-\lambda)\boldsymbol{x}_2)=\lambda f(\boldsymbol{x}_1)+(1-\lambda)f(\boldsymbol{x}_2)$

questions.question: Let $f(x)=\sqrt{x}$ on the domain $D=[0,4]$. Which point of $\mathbb{R}^2$ lies in $\operatorname{Epi}(f)$?
For $f(x)=x^2-2x$ on $\mathbb{R}$, which set is the vertical slice $\{y\in\mathbb{R}\colon(3,y)\in\operatorname{Epi}(f)\}$ of the epigraph above $x=3$?
options: $[3,\infty)$

questions.question: For $f(x)=x^2$ on $\mathbb{R}$, which set is the horizontal slice $\{x\in\mathbb{R}\colon(x,4)\in\operatorname{Epi}(f)\}$ of the epigraph at height $4$?
options: $(-\infty,-2]\cup[2,\infty)$

questions.question: For the affine function $f(x)=3x-1$ on $\mathbb{R}$, which subset of $\mathbb{R}^2$ is $\operatorname{Epi}(f)$?
options: $\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon 3x-y\geq1\}$
$\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon 3x-y=1\}$
$\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon 3x-y\leq1\}$
$\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon 3x-y\leq-1\}$

questions.question: Let $f(x_1,x_2)=x_1^2+x_2^2$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$. The points $(1,0,2)$ and $(-1,2,8)$ of $\mathbb{R}^3$ lie in $\operatorname{Epi}(f)$, since $f(1,0)=1\leq2$ and $f(-1,2)=5\leq8$. Which is their combination with weights $\tfrac{1}{4}$ and $\tfrac{3}{4}$, and what does the membership check give?
options: $(-\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{3}{2},\tfrac{13}{2})$; it lies in $\operatorname{Epi}(f)$ since $f(-\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{3}{2})=\tfrac{5}{2}\leq\tfrac{13}{2}$.
$(-\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{3}{2},\tfrac{5}{2})$; its height is the value $f(-\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{3}{2})=\tfrac{5}{2}$, so it lies on the graph.
$(-\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{3}{2},4)$; its height combines the function values, $\tfrac{1}{4}\cdot1+\tfrac{3}{4}\cdot5=4\geq\tfrac{5}{2}$.
$(\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{7}{2})$, which is in $\operatorname{Epi}(f)$ because $\tfrac{7}{2}\geq f(\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{1}{2})=\tfrac{1}{2}$.

questions.question: For $f(\boldsymbol{x})=\|\boldsymbol{x}\|$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$, the epigraph $\operatorname{Epi}(f)$ is a solid cone with apex at the origin, and it is a convex set. Which conclusion about $f$ is correct?
options: $f$ is strictly convex, because its epigraph is a convex set.
$f$ is not convex, because the epigraph has a sharp apex where $f$ is not differentiable.
$f$ is strictly convex away from the origin, since the apex is the only corner of the graph.
$f$ is convex but not strictly convex: its graph contains straight half-lines from the origin.

questions.question: For convex $f_1,f_2\colon\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$, the maximum $\max\{f_1,f_2\}$ is always convex, but the minimum need not be, as $\min\{x^2,(x-2)^2\}$ shows. Which epigraph fact explains why the argument for the maximum fails for the minimum?
options: $\operatorname{Epi}(\min\{f_1,f_2\})=\operatorname{Epi}(f_1)\cap\operatorname{Epi}(f_2)$, and this intersection need not be convex.
$\operatorname{Epi}(\min\{f_1,f_2\})=\operatorname{Epi}(f_1)\cup\operatorname{Epi}(f_2)$, and a union of convex sets need not be convex.
$\operatorname{Epi}(\min\{f_1,f_2\})$ is convex, but a convex epigraph forces convexity only for differentiable functions.
$\operatorname{Epi}(\min\{f_1,f_2\})=\operatorname{Epi}(f_1)+\operatorname{Epi}(f_2)$, and a sum of convex sets need not be convex.

questions.question: A function $f\colon[-1,1]\to\mathbb{R}$ is discontinuous at the interior point $0$ of its domain. What can be concluded about the convexity of $\operatorname{Epi}(f)$?
options: It is not convex, because a convex function is continuous at every interior point of its domain.
It can still be convex, provided the jump at $0$ goes upwards rather than downwards.
It can still be convex, provided $f$ is convex on $[-1,0]$ and on $(0,1]$ separately.
Nothing, because the epigraph criterion for convexity applies only to continuous functions.

questions.question: For $f(x)=x^3$ on $D=[-1,1]$, the points $(-1,-1)$ and $(0,0)$ lie on the graph of $f$. Which statement about their midpoint and the convexity of $f$ is correct?
options: $(-\tfrac{1}{2},-\tfrac{1}{2})\in\operatorname{Epi}(f)$, since $-\tfrac{1}{2}\geq f(-1)=-1$; the pair shows nothing.
$(-\tfrac{1}{2},-\tfrac{1}{2})\notin\operatorname{Epi}(f)$, so $f$ is concave rather than convex on $[-1,1]$.
$(-\tfrac{1}{2},-\tfrac{1}{2})\notin\operatorname{Epi}(f)$, since $f(-\tfrac{1}{2})=-\tfrac{1}{8}$; so $f$ is not convex.
$(-\tfrac{1}{2},-\tfrac{1}{2})\in\operatorname{Epi}(f)$, since $f(-\tfrac{1}{2})=-\tfrac{1}{8}$ is less than $-\tfrac{1}{2}$.

questions.question: Let $V\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2$ be the closed triangle with vertices $(-1,1)$, $(1,1)$ and $(0,0)$, a convex set. On the projection $D$ of $V$ onto the first coordinate, put $f(x)=\inf\{y\in\mathbb{R}\colon(x,y)\in V\}$. Which is $f$?
Which subset of $\mathbb{R}^2$ equals $\operatorname{Epi}(f)$ for some set $D\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ and some function $f\colon D\to\mathbb{R}$?
options: $\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon x^2\leq y\leq4\}$
$\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon x\geq0,\ y\geq x^2\}$
$\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon y>x^2\}$
$\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon x^2+y^2\geq1\}$

questions.question: Let $V\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}$ be convex with projection $D$ onto $\mathbb{R}^n$, and $f(\boldsymbol{x})=\inf\{y\in\mathbb{R}\colon(\boldsymbol{x},y)\in V\}$. The result that $f$ is convex on $D$ assumes this infimum is greater than $-\infty$ for every $\boldsymbol{x}\in D$. What does this assumption secure?
options: That $f$ is real-valued; for $V=\{(x,y)\colon y\leq0\}$ every infimum would be $-\infty$.
That $D$ is convex; without it the projection of a convex set $V$ can fail to be convex.
That $V$ is closed, which the proof needs in order to pick a lowest point in each slice.
That $V$ equals $\operatorname{Epi}(f)$, so that the epigraph criterion can be applied to $V$.

questions.question: Let $D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be a set that is not convex, and let $f\colon D\to\mathbb{R}$ be any function. Which statement about the convexity of $\operatorname{Epi}(f)$ is correct?
options: It is convex if $f$ is constant, since a constant function has no curvature at all.
It is convex if $f$ is the restriction to $D$ of a convex function on $\mathbb{R}^n$.
It may or may not be convex; the equivalence with convexity of $f$ is just unavailable.
It is never convex, since projecting it onto $\mathbb{R}^n$ gives the nonconvex set $D$.

questions.question: Let $f\colon[0,1]\to\mathbb{R}$ be given by $f(x)=0$ for $0\leq x<1$ and $f(1)=2$, so $f$ jumps at the endpoint $1$. Is $\operatorname{Epi}(f)$ a convex set?
options: No: a convex function must be continuous on all of $[0,1]$, including the endpoint $1$.
No: the midpoint of the points $(0,0)$ and $(1,0)$ lies outside $\operatorname{Epi}(f)$.
Yes: all its points have $y\geq0$, and above every $x<1$ membership only needs $y\geq0$.
Only after redefining $f(1)=0$, the one value that makes $f$ continuous at $1$.

questions.question: The set $V=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon x^2<y<1\}$ is convex. On the projection $D$ of $V$ onto the first coordinate, put $f(x)=\inf\{y\in\mathbb{R}\colon(x,y)\in V\}$. Which statement about $D$ and $f$ is correct?
options: No convex function results, because no slice of $V$ contains its own infimum.
$D=(-1,1)$ and $f(x)=x^2$, which is convex although no infimum is attained.
$D=[-1,1]$ and $f(x)=x^2$, since the parabola meets the line $y=1$ at $x=\pm1$.
$D=(-1,1)$ and $f(x)=1$, the height that bounds each slice of $V$ from above.
